platforms.title: A Stuffy Nose Might Be Behind Your Worst Airplane Ear Pain
platforms.meta_description: Airplane ear happens when a blocked eustachian tube can't match cabin pressure. CDC and MedlinePlus tips on gum, yawning, decongestants and when to call.
platforms.body_html:
Most people who fly know the feeling: the plane starts its descent, your ears fill up as if you were underwater, and then a sharp, pressing pain sets in on one side. Some flights it barely registers; other times it lingers well after you land. The difference is often not the flight at all but the state of your nose. Congestion from a cold or allergies is one of the main reasons the same flight hurts more one week than another, and it is something you can plan around.

Why a Blocked Nose Turns Pressure Into Pain

Your middle ear, the small air-filled space behind the eardrum, connects to the back of the nose through a narrow channel called the eustachian tube. Swallowing or yawning opens that tube and lets air move in and out, so the pressure on both sides of the eardrum stays equal. MedlinePlus, the US National Library of Medicine's consumer site, explains that if the eustachian tube is blocked, the pressure difference can cause barotrauma, the medical name for pressure-related ear injury.

On a plane, that pressure changes quickly. According to the CDC Yellow Book chapter on air travel, US regulations require commercial aircraft to keep cabin pressure at the equivalent of no more than 8,000 feet (2,440 m), and cabins typically sit at 6,000 to 8,000 feet. During the climb the cabin pressure falls fast, and during descent it rises fast. The CDC notes that barotrauma most commonly affects the middle ear and happens when the tube is blocked and you cannot equalize with the cabin.

That is where your nose comes in. MedlinePlus says you are more likely to develop barotrauma if you have nasal congestion from allergies, colds or an upper respiratory infection, because swelling at the back of the nose narrows the opening of the tube.

Most Cases Are Mild, and Simple Steps Help

The reassuring part first. The CDC describes middle ear barotrauma as usually not severe or dangerous, and MedlinePlus calls it a benign, self-limited condition in which hearing loss is almost always temporary. Rare complications listed by the CDC include dizziness, hearing loss, a perforated eardrum or permanent tinnitus, which is why it is still worth preventing.

The self-care steps MedlinePlus lists all aim to open the eustachian tube:

  • chew gum or suck on a hard candy
  • yawn
  • inhale, then gently exhale while holding your nostrils closed and your mouth shut
  • for infants and small children, nursing or taking sips of a drink

Timing matters as much as technique. MedlinePlus specifically advises: do not sleep as the plane prepares to land, and repeat these steps through the descent. If you are a habitual sleeper on flights, set a reminder or ask your travel companion to nudge you when the descent announcement comes.

Plan for the Congestion, Not Just the Flight

Because congestion is the multiplier, the most useful preparation happens before you board. MedlinePlus notes that nasal decongestants, as a spray or tablets, can be used before altitude changes. The CDC says travelers with ear, nose and sinus infections or severe congestion might choose to postpone flying to prevent pain or injury, or use oral or nasal decongestants to help, and that people with allergies should keep taking their regular allergy medicines. Decongestants are not right for everyone, so check with a pharmacist or doctor if you have other health conditions or take other medicines.

If you already have a perforated eardrum, the NHS says it is safe to fly. The exception is after surgery to repair the eardrum (myringoplasty): in that case, do not fly until you are told it is safe.

When Airplane Ear Needs a Doctor

Try the home measures first. MedlinePlus advises contacting a provider if the discomfort does not ease after a few hours, or if new symptoms develop, especially:

  • drainage or bleeding from the ear
  • fever
  • severe ear pain

For people who are prone to barotrauma and must change altitude often, MedlinePlus notes that ear tubes placed in the eardrum are sometimes an option, which is a conversation to have with an ear, nose and throat specialist.

A quick look back at what to check before your next flight: is your nose clear, or do you need a plan for congestion? Do you have gum or a candy within reach for the descent? Will you be awake when the plane starts preparing to land? And after landing, are you watching for fluid, fever or pain that is not settling within a few hours? This article is general information and does not replace advice from your own doctor or pharmacist.

Sources: CDC Yellow Book 2026, "Air Travel" (Sundari R Mase et al.); MedlinePlus, "Ear barotrauma" (reviewed 4/29/2026); NHS, "Perforated eardrum" (reviewed 19 April 2023).
